Sam Snead. Slammin' Sam. An American professional golfer with one of the longest competitive careers in golf history, spanning over five decades. His 7 major championships and 82 professional tournament victories made him one of the most prolific winners in the sport, known for his graceful, powerful swing and accessibility to fans.

He won 7 major championships: 3 Masters in 1949, 1952, and 1954, 3 PGA Championships in 1942, 1949, and 1951, and 1 British Open in 1946. He won 82 official PGA Tour events, tied with Jack Nicklaus for the most in tour history by official count. Snead competed professionally from 1936 until 1974, demonstrating extraordinary longevity—he was competitive across six different decades. He was famous for his natural, effortless swing and ability to adapt his game across different course conditions and styles.

What remains one of golf's most notable what-ifs is that Snead never won the US Open despite finishing second four times. He pioneered the Senior PGA Tour upon its formation, continuing to win tournaments well into his 60s. Known for his folksy personality, colorful attire, and connection with working-class fans who saw him as accessible, Snead was a contemporary rival of Ben Hogan during golf's golden age, competed with Byron Nelson in the 1940s era, and saw Arnold Palmer succeed him during his extended career.
